title: A la recherche d'une perle
summary: "A la recherche d'une perle" by Henriette Bezançon is a novel written in the early 20th century. It centers on Jeanne Ferval, a Breton girl raised by her beloved grandfather, who must leave her quiet life for Paris after his death and adapt to a distant father, a self-absorbed stepmother, and two very different sisters. Alongside Jeanne’s quiet resilience and piety, the narrative introduces Mme Brumme, a gracious widow grieving a son who died heroically in the Titanic disaster, suggesting a story about conscience, charity, and the testing of character in modern city life. At the start of the story, Jeanne leaves Quimper in tears, recalling her gentle upbringing by her poet grandfather and the guidance of the Abbé Lejal. On the train she silently bonds with a noble woman in deep mourning, later finding the woman’s memorial card for a son who gave his place in a Titanic lifeboat. Arriving at the Gare Saint-Lazare, Jeanne meets her well-meaning but hesitant father and is presented to her elegant, calculating stepmother Valérie, the precocious half-sister Georgette, and the kind, sensible stepsister Marie-Louise. A thin, showy Parisian dinner and a chill welcome underline the clash between Jeanne’s simple, devout habits and the family’s life of appearances and fashionable “Minerva” lectures. Settling into a small room, she rebuilds a corner of her past with a crucifix, books, and the found memorial card, while Marie-Louise befriends her and Georgette needles her. The focus then shifts to Mme Brumme, whose serene faith after her son’s heroic death sustains her daily works of mercy, shown in a tender visit to a destitute elderly protégée—hinting that Jeanne’s path and this widow’s quiet strength may soon meet.
